q: An object falling through a fluid reaches its terminal velocity when:
o: The drag force becomes greater than its weight
The net force on it becomes zero
Its acceleration becomes equal to g
x: At terminal velocity the upward forces (drag, plus upthrust) balance the weight, so the net force and acceleration are zero and the speed stays constant. For a body falling from rest the drag never exceeds the weight.

q: Steady (streamline) flow of a fluid means that:
o: The fluid moves with the same speed everywhere
The velocity of the fluid at any given point does not change with time
The fluid particles move in circles
x: In steady flow every particle that passes a given point has the same velocity there as those before it. The speed may still differ from one point to another.

q: According to Bernoulli's effect, in the horizontal flow of a fluid, where the speed of the fluid is higher the pressure is:
x: From P + ½ρv² = constant for horizontal flow, a larger v means a smaller P. This is Bernoulli's effect.

q: According to Stokes' law, the drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving with speed v through a fluid of viscosity η is:
x: Stokes' law is F = 6πηrv: drag is directly proportional to radius, speed and viscosity. It holds for small spheres moving slowly, in laminar flow.

q: An ideal fluid is said to be incompressible. This means that:
o: Its velocity stays constant throughout the flow
Its density stays constant throughout the flow
Its pressure is the same everywhere
x: Incompressible means its volume, and so its density, does not change with pressure. Zero viscosity is the separate non-viscous condition.

q: An aeroplane wing (aerofoil) is shaped so that air flows faster over its upper surface than under it. This produces lift because:
o: The pressure above the wing is higher than the pressure below it
The pressure above the wing is lower than the pressure below it
The air above the wing is denser
The drag on the wing acts upward
x: By Bernoulli's effect the faster air above the wing has lower pressure. The higher pressure below pushes the wing upward, giving lift.

q: A raindrop starts falling from rest through still air. Which describes its acceleration as it falls?
o: It decreases from g to zero
It stays equal to g throughout
It increases from zero to g
It decreases from g to a constant non-zero value
x: At the start the speed, and so the drag, is zero, so the acceleration is g. As the speed rises the drag grows, the net force falls, and the acceleration falls to zero at terminal velocity.

q: Non-viscous flow of an ideal fluid means that:
o: There is no internal friction between adjacent layers of the fluid
The flow speed is the same at every point
x: Viscosity is internal friction between layers; a non-viscous fluid has none, so no energy is lost to friction as it flows. Incompressibility is a different property.

q: A Venturi meter is used to:
o: Measure the speed (flow rate) of a fluid in a pipe from a pressure difference
Measure the viscosity of a liquid
Measure the density of a gas
Measure blood pressure directly inside an artery
x: A Venturi meter has a narrow throat in a pipe. The pressure difference between the wide part and the throat, used with Bernoulli's equation and continuity, gives the flow speed.

q: Ignoring upthrust, the terminal velocity of a small sphere is v_t = 2ρgr²/9η. A sphere of the same material but twice the radius has a terminal velocity that is:
x: v_t is proportional to r², so doubling r multiplies v_t by 2² = 4. The weight grows eight times (∝ r³), but the drag also grows with r.

q: In steady flow, two streamlines can never cross each other because:
o: The fluid would become compressed at that point
The viscosity would become infinite there
At the crossing point a fluid particle would have two directions of velocity
The pressure would become zero there
x: The tangent to a streamline gives the direction of the velocity. If two streamlines crossed, a particle at that point would have two velocities at once, which is impossible.

q: In a perfume spray (atomiser), squeezing the bulb sends a jet of air across the top of a tube dipping into the liquid. The liquid rises up the tube because:
o: The fast air raises the pressure at the top of the tube
The fast air lowers the pressure at the top of the tube, so the higher pressure on the liquid surface pushes it up
The liquid is attracted by the moving air
x: Fast-moving air has low pressure. Atmospheric pressure on the liquid in the bottle is then greater and forces the liquid up the tube, where the jet breaks it into droplets.

q: A small sphere of radius 1 × 10⁻³ m moves at a steady 0.02 m s⁻¹ through oil of viscosity 0.5 Pa s. Using Stokes' law, the drag force on it is:
In laminar flow:
o: The fluid moves in irregular whirls and eddies
The fluid particles move randomly in all directions
The velocity at a point changes erratically
Layers of fluid slide smoothly past one another
x: Laminar (streamline) flow is smooth and orderly: adjacent layers slide past each other without mixing. Eddies and erratic changes describe turbulent flow.

q: For an ideal fluid flowing through a horizontal tube, Bernoulli's equation is:
x: For a horizontal tube the ρgh term is the same at both ends and drops out, leaving P + ½ρv² = constant.

q: A sphere of radius 3 × 10⁻³ m and density 3000 kg m⁻³ falls through a liquid of density 1000 kg m⁻³ and viscosity 2 Pa s. Its terminal velocity is v_t = 2(ρ − σ)gr²/9η, where σ is the liquid's density. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², v_t is:
x: v_t = 2 × (3000 − 1000) × 10 × 9 × 10⁻⁶ / (9 × 2) = 0.36/18 = 0.02 m s⁻¹. Using 3000 instead of (ρ − σ) gives 0.03 m s⁻¹; dropping the factor 2 gives 0.01 m s⁻¹.

q: A raindrop of mass 2 g falls through air at its terminal velocity. Ignoring the upthrust of the air, the viscous drag on it is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so drag = weight = mg = 0.002 × 10 = 0.02 N. Using 2 kg for 2 g gives 20 N; forgetting g gives 0.002 N.

q: From Stokes' law F = 6πηrv, the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity η can be written as:
x: η = F/(6πrv) has unit N/(m × m s⁻¹) = (kg m s⁻²)/(m² s⁻¹) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹, which is the same as Pa s. kg m⁻¹ s⁻² is the unit of pressure, the tempting slip.

q: Water flows steadily at 1.5 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of diameter 4 cm, which then narrows to a diameter of 2 cm. The speed of the water in the narrow part is:
x: By continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ and A ∝ d², so v₂ = 1.5 × (4/2)² = 1.5 × 4 = 6 m s⁻¹. Taking area proportional to diameter gives 3 m s⁻¹.

q: Water comes out of a hose of cross-sectional area 2 cm² at a speed of 5 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to fill a 10-litre bucket?
x: Flow rate Q = Av = 2 × 10⁻⁴ m² × 5 m s⁻¹ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 1 litre per second, so 10 litres take 10 s. Converting cm² to m² with 10⁻⁶ instead of 10⁻⁴ gives 1000 s; forgetting that 1 m³ is 1000 litres gives the other values.

q: The equation of continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, for an incompressible fluid follows from the conservation of:
x: The mass of fluid entering a pipe section per second must equal the mass leaving it; with constant density this gives A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. Conservation of energy leads to Bernoulli's equation, the usual confusion.

q: A large open tank is filled with water. A small hole is made in its side 5 m below the water surface. By Torricelli's theorem, the speed of the water leaving the hole is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 100 m s⁻¹; leaving out the 2 gives √50 = 5√2 m s⁻¹.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe. Its speed rises from 2 m s⁻¹ in the wide part to 4 m s⁻¹ in the narrow part. The pressure in the wide part exceeds that in the narrow part by:
x: Bernoulli for a horizontal pipe: P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 4) = 6000 Pa. Using (v₂ − v₁)² gives 2000 Pa; forgetting the ½ gives 12000 Pa.

q: According to Archimedes' principle, the upthrust on a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid is equal to the:
o: Weight of the fluid displaced by the body
Pressure of the fluid at the depth of the body
x: Upthrust equals the weight of the fluid the body displaces. It equals the body's own weight only when the body floats, which is the common slip.

q: A metal block of volume 2 × 10⁻³ m³ is completely immersed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. The upthrust on it is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Upthrust = ρVg = 1000 × 2 × 10⁻³ × 10 = 20 N. Forgetting g gives 2 N.

q: A 5 kg stone of density 2500 kg m⁻³ hangs from a spring balance, completely immersed in water (density 1000 kg m⁻³). The balance reads (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Volume = 5/2500 = 2 × 10⁻³ m³, so upthrust = 1000 × 2 × 10⁻³ × 10 = 20 N; reading = 50 − 20 = 30 N. 20 N is only the upthrust; adding it to the weight gives 70 N.

q: A block of wood of density 600 kg m⁻³ floats in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. The fraction of its volume that is below the water surface is:
x: Floating: weight = upthrust, so ρ_wood V g = ρ_water V_sub g and V_sub/V = 600/1000 = 60 %. 40 % is the fraction above the surface.

q: A solid floats in water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) with three-quarters of its volume submerged. In another liquid it floats with five-sixths of its volume submerged. The density of the second liquid is:
x: Solid's density = ¾ × 1000 = 750 kg m⁻³; in the liquid 750 = (5/6)ρ_L, so ρ_L = 750 × 6/5 = 900 kg m⁻³. Multiplying by 5/6 instead of dividing gives 625 kg m⁻³.

q: A solid weighs 12 N in air and 8 N when completely immersed in water. The relative density (specific gravity) of the solid is:
x: Relative density = weight in air ÷ loss of weight in water = 12/(12 − 8) = 12/4 = 3. Dividing by the weight in water gives 12/8 = 1.5.

q: A wooden raft of volume 0.5 m³ and density 600 kg m⁻³ floats in fresh water (density 1000 kg m⁻³). What is the largest mass of load that can be placed on top of it before the raft is completely submerged?
x: Fully submerged, the raft displaces 1000 × 0.5 = 500 kg of water; the raft itself has mass 600 × 0.5 = 300 kg, so the load can be 500 − 300 = 200 kg. Forgetting the raft's own mass gives 500 kg.
